concepts.decision: Put security stories, acceptance criteria, threat-model changes, and security tests into each increment rather than a final hardening phase.
concepts.definition: An iterative approach that delivers small increments through collaborative planning, building, testing, and feedback cycles.
concepts.failureExample: A rapid sprint cadence with security work kept in a separate backlog ships repeated unreviewed exposure.
concepts.label: Agile

concepts.decision: Use when controlled requirements, documentation, and formal gates suit the mission; still manage rework and security changes across phases.
concepts.definition: A lifecycle approach that organizes work into formal phases and baselines, commonly with approval milestones before transition.
concepts.failureExample: Deferring security until a final phase embeds missing requirements into design and makes remediation expensive.
concepts.label: Waterfall

concepts.decision: Use shared operational telemetry and deployment practice to shorten feedback, while retaining security requirements and accountable change decisions.
concepts.definition: A delivery/operating model that joins development, operations, and often quality practices to improve flow, reliability, and feedback.
concepts.failureExample: Fast deployment without production ownership or rollback turns operational feedback into repeated outages.
concepts.label: Devops

concepts.decision: Automate repeatable checks early and keep human ownership for design tradeoffs, exceptions, incident response, and acceptance.
concepts.definition: DevOps practices with security collaboration, security criteria, and appropriate automated/manual checks integrated through delivery and operations.
concepts.failureExample: Treating a passed scanner as authorization to release can miss a changed trust boundary or unmet privacy requirement.
concepts.label: Devsecops

concepts.decision: Use common security standards, architecture decisions, dependency visibility, and cross-team acceptance evidence when one team’s change affects another.
concepts.definition: Coordination practices that align multiple Agile teams, shared dependencies, and integrated delivery outcomes.
concepts.failureExample: One team can safely pass its service tests while breaking a shared authorization contract used by another team.
concepts.label: Scaled Agile

concepts.decision: Use it to prioritize process improvement; pair it with change-specific product evidence and risk decisions.
concepts.definition: Capability Maturity Model: a framework for assessing whether development processes are repeatable, defined, measured, and improving.
concepts.failureExample: A mature documentation process can repeatedly produce a release with an untested authorization flaw.
concepts.label: Cmm

concepts.decision: Use it to identify practice gaps and a realistic improvement roadmap, not to declare an individual system free of vulnerabilities.
concepts.definition: Software Assurance Maturity Model: a maturity framework for evaluating and improving software-security practices across the development organization.
concepts.failureExample: A high SAMM practice level does not prove that a newly added endpoint has been threat-modeled.
concepts.label: Samm

concepts.decision: Link the change to code/configuration, tests, approver, deployment owner, monitoring, rollback, and retrospective; use a governed emergency path when needed.
concepts.definition: Controlled transition from a current software/configuration state to a future state through scoped request, risk review, authorization, implementation, verification, and learning.
concepts.failureExample: An urgent patch with no rollback owner can convert a vulnerability response into prolonged service loss.
concepts.label: Change Management

concepts.decision: Treat production signals and incidents as input to risk, backlog, design, and lifecycle decisions; retain responsibility through retirement.
concepts.definition: Post-production activity that monitors, patches, recovers, manages vulnerabilities and changes, maintains ownership, and retires software safely.
concepts.failureExample: Leaving a superseded service account or secret active after retirement extends attack surface indefinitely.
concepts.label: Operations Maintenance

misconceptions.claim: DevSecOps means every security control must be fully automated.
misconceptions.correction: Automation improves consistency and speed, but design judgment, exceptions, incident response, and accountability remain human responsibilities.

outcome: Select lifecycle gates and operational feedback appropriate to delivery speed, risk, and system change.

sections.body: Waterfall uses formal phase baselines; Agile iterates in small increments; DevOps joins delivery and operations; DevSecOps makes security collaboration and automation explicit; scaled frameworks coordinate many teams. CMM and SAMM can reveal process capability and improvement priorities, but maturity scores do not prove a product is secure.
keyPoints: The method changes timing and evidence, not the need for security decisions.
Maturity models assess capability and repeatability, not residual risk alone.
Automated checks should be fast enough to influence the change.
sections.title: Choose feedback and governance deliberately

sections.body: Secure delivery requires environment separation, release authorization, configuration baselines, rollback, vulnerability response, monitoring, incident feedback, maintenance ownership, and retirement actions. Emergency changes need an explicit path with retrospective evidence rather than bypassing accountability.
keyPoints: Deployment is a transition into operational assurance, not its endpoint.
Change records connect code, configuration, approver, test evidence, and rollback.
Retirement revokes access, handles data and secrets, and preserves required evidence.
sections.title: Preserve assurance after release
